name: AI and Faith: An Interfaith Network's AI Ethics Resources and Reviews
title: AI and Faith: An Interfaith Network's AI Ethics Resources and Reviews
answer: AI and Faith is a Washington nonprofit network that brings AI professionals, ethicists, theologians, clergy, and faith leaders together on the ethical deployment of AI. Its website collects interviews, annual reflections, essays, and book reviews. The most useful point for religious organisations is its argument that faith communities represent meaning, common life, relationships, and morality, and that their long histories of helping people and promoting human development let them perceive new ways AI can benefit society and help technologists consider the common good.

sections.body: AI and Faith publishes the site. The pages reviewed describe AI and Faith as a Washington nonprofit that incorporated, established a governing board, and secured IRS tax exemption status. It began when a community of AI professionals, related professions, ethicists, theologians, and philosophers gathered in January 2018. It gathered 26 Founding Experts and seven cross-disciplinary and cross-faith institutional partners in the Seattle area who met bimonthly, and it later says its community of Founding Experts grew to nearly fifty experts around the country. The pages reviewed include an interview with Brian Green on the Vatican Conference on AI and the Common Good, a reflection on 2018 and look ahead to 2019, an essay titled Means and Ends for AI and for Faith, and book reviews of Human Compatible, Prediction Machines, and AI Superpowers. The content dates from around 2018 and 2019, though the site was read on 2026-09-29.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The interview with Brian Green covers his technology ethics work, including his work at Santa Clara University and the Markkula Center for Applied Ethics. He designed an AI ethics course covering 16 areas of concern, wrote an article on 12 concerns, and produced a top ten list. He argues faith communities represent meaning, common life, relationships, and morality. AI-powered addictive online games can make money but may destroy relationships and de-skill people from social interaction. Faith communities have long histories of helping people and promoting human development, so they can perceive new ways AI might benefit society and help technologists consider the common good. The 2018 reflection notes advances in data capture, predictive analytics, deep learning, and virtual reality, the Cambridge Analytica fallout, Google's employee revolt and do no harm principles, California's data ownership stance, Chinese AI surveillance, Partnership on AI growth from 25 to over 70 partners. It says none of Partnership on AI's new partners brought a formal faith perspective, and that many Big Tech leaders seem guided by a materialist orientation. The essay Means and Ends argues AI and faith share areas of concern and some common ends and means, though they differ in approach and practice. It says both seek to understand human behavior and the world, while faith weighs AI's patterns and insights against belief systems about human origin, human nature, good and evil, justice, and the universe. The book reviews summarize Stuart Russell's Human Compatible, Prediction Machines, and Kai-Fu Lee's AI Superpowers.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: Brian Green says he has worked on technology ethics, including AI, for about 15 years, began teaching at Santa Clara University's School of Engineering in 2011, joined the Markkula Center for Applied Ethics in 2013, and helped the center join the Partnership on AI in 2017. His AI ethics course covers 16 areas of concern, he wrote an article on 12 concerns, and he produced a Markkula Center top ten list. AI and Faith says it gathered 26 Founding Experts and seven cross-disciplinary and cross-faith institutional partners in the Seattle area, and later says its community of Founding Experts grew to nearly fifty experts around the country. It says Partnership on AI partners grew from 25 to over 70 global partners by the end of 2018. Kai-Fu Lee estimates that within ten to twenty years AI will be capable of automating close to half of all jobs in the United States, though he does not expect actual job losses to be that high. Stuart Russell proposes Three Principles for Beneficial Machines: the machine's only objective is to maximize the realization of human preferences, the machine is initially uncertain about what those preferences are, and the ultimate source of information about human preferences is human behavior. Prediction Machines boils down to three foundational insights: AI brings prediction, AI makes prediction radically less expensive, and when prediction is cheaper, complements such as judgment become more valuable. The essay quotes Eugene Peterson in Living the Message on pages 244 to 45 saying the two essentials of human fullness are intimacy and transcendancy.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For churches and faith organisations, this source is useful because it gives a vocabulary and a set of examples for engaging AI ethics from within a faith perspective. The Brian Green interview directly addresses why faith communities matter to AI ethics, arguing that they represent meaning, common life, relationships, and morality, and that their histories of helping people and promoting human development let them see new ways AI might benefit society. The 2018 reflection shows an interfaith network forming around these questions, with experts, institutional partners, conferences, and a newsletter, and it notes that Partnership on AI's new partners did not appear to bring a formal faith perspective. That gap is an opportunity for religious organisations. The essay Means and Ends helps faith leaders connect AI's pattern recognition and insights to long-developed beliefs about human origin, human nature, good and evil, justice, and the universe. The book reviews translate major AI ethics and economics arguments, including Russell's Three Principles, Prediction Machines on judgment as a complement to cheap prediction, and Lee's job automation estimates, into material a clergyperson or faith-based ethicist can use in teaching, preaching, or institutional discernment. The source does not offer implementation steps, but it does show how faith communities can join the common good conversation.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Churches and Faith Organisations

sections.body: The pages reviewed are commentary, interviews, essays, and book reviews rather than original research, denominational policy, or technical guidance. They date from around 2018 and 2019, so some examples and claims, such as the state of Partnership on AI or Chinese AI surveillance, are dated. The source reflects the perspective of AI and Faith, a nonprofit network with a stated mission, and it does not claim to speak for all faith traditions. It does not provide step-by-step guidance for congregations adopting AI, nor does it cover specific church software, data protection rules, or pastoral care tools. The book reviews summarize other authors' arguments rather than testing them. The AI Superpowers review focuses on economic and geopolitical claims, not faith applications. The site is not commercial, but it is partial and early-stage, as its 2019 plans to secure sustainable funding and grow its community suggest.
